task: Write one sentence of your own using the word insoluble. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know insoluble should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The strange medieval manuscript's cipher has defeated professional codebreakers for over a century, and many experts now believe the puzzle is simply insoluble.
A tricky problem takes cleverness but can eventually be cracked; an insoluble one has no solution to find at all.
Calling a situation hopeless goes even further than insoluble, suggesting that nothing about it, not even the outlook, can ever improve.

Unsolvable means exactly what it says: no solution exists to be found. It is the plain-English twin of insoluble, and in most sentences the two are interchangeable. Insoluble is the more formal, test-favored word, the one writers reach for with grand problems like an insoluble paradox.

Unanswerable applies to questions: an unanswerable question has no answer that can ever settle it. Insoluble applies to problems, puzzles, and disputes, things that demand a solution rather than an answer. A riddle with no answer is unanswerable; a conflict no proposal can fix is insoluble.

Irresolvable describes a disagreement or conflict that cannot be settled between the people in it; an irresolvable feud grinds on because no compromise can end it. It needs parties and a standoff. Insoluble is wider, covering any problem or puzzle that has no solution at all.

After one honest conversation, the roommates managed to resolve their long-running disagreement about chores.
Insoluble means impossible to solve.

For three generations, two branches of the Alvarez family have argued over who rightfully inherited the lake cottage, and every lawyer who reads the tangled, contradictory will declares the dispute insoluble.
The will is so contradictory that no reading of it can settle who owns the cottage, meaning the dispute has no possible solution.
A problem or dispute with no solution to be found is exactly what insoluble describes.
Insoluble describes a problem, dispute, or puzzle that has no solution at all: an insoluble mystery, an insoluble conflict.
Keep it distinct from intractable, which is broader and describes anything, including people and ongoing situations, that resists being managed or controlled even if a solution might exist somewhere.
Insoluble also has a chemistry sense, 'unable to be dissolved,' but on the SAT the unsolvable-problem sense is the one to know.

In 1882 the mathematician Ferdinand von Lindemann settled a puzzle that had tormented geometers since ancient Greece: squaring the circle.
The challenge sounds simple -- using only a compass and straightedge, draw a square with exactly the same area as a given circle.
For two thousand years, professionals and cranks alike filled notebooks with near-misses, each certain the right construction was one clever step away.
Lindemann proved the problem is insoluble: because pi is a transcendental number, no finite construction with those tools can ever produce the square.
The proof did not merely report that no one had solved it yet; it showed that no one ever could, and the two-thousand-year hunt was over.
